title: the four mahavakyas — prajnanam brahma
tomorrow: the text asks one question twice. why won't the first answer do?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the four mahavakyas reached the Aitareya's opening: fire became speech, wind became breath, and the powers moved into a person. Today, that same person, and a meal that won't sit still.

One in the morning, and the phone is playing cooking videos. Butter hissing in a pan. Someone tearing open warm bread. A whole video of it, and the stomach is exactly as empty as before. The Aitareya Upanishad tells a story about that very problem. The self has just made a person and moved the powers in. Then it makes food. And the food, the text says, turns around and runs.
screen: `COOKING VIDEOS AT ONE A.M.` → `STILL HUNGRY.` → `THE FOOD TURNS AND RUNS.`

segments.voice: So the chase begins. First the self tries to catch the food with speech, and can't. The text adds a line that's funny on purpose: if speech had caught it, a person would be full just from saying the word food. Next, breath. If breath had caught it, smelling food would be enough. Then the eye: seeing food would fill you. The ear: hearing about food would do it. Touch. Then the mind: just thinking about a meal would be a meal. One by one, every power the person has reaches out, and the food slips away. At last the self tries apana, the breath that draws in and down, the one that takes food in. That one catches it. Why tell a story about lunch in a book famous for one of the great sayings? Look at its shape. Each power is real, and each does its own job well. The eye really sees. The mind really pictures. But not one of them, alone, is the whole person, and not one of them, alone, is satisfied. The chase clears the table for the question this week keeps asking: if every power is only one part, what knows all of them at once? The Aitareya's answer is prajnanam brahma, the knowing is Brahman. Not the eye, not the ear, not the thought: the knowing they all report to.
screen: `SPEECH, BREATH, EYE, EAR: ALL MISS.` · `THE MIND MISSES TOO.` · `APANA CATCHES IT.` · `NO ONE POWER IS THE WHOLE PERSON.` · then, large: `PRAJNANAM BRAHMA.`

segments.voice: If there's something to eat nearby, a raisin, a cracker, a sip of tea, first just look at it. Then smell it. Then taste it, slowly. At each step, notice which power is reaching out, and notice the quiet knowing that's aware of every one of them.
The four mahavakyas: the great sayings. This week's is prajnanam brahma, and today's story sets the table for it. Every power reaches; something knows the reaching.
Your line: the four mahavakyas — prajnanam brahma. No single power was the whole person. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Students of the Aitareya Upanishad read its opening stories, the powers entering the person and the chase after food, with a teacher as the setting for the great saying prajnanam brahma.

myth: the Upanishads treat the body and its senses as unimportant

it jokes the other way: if the mind had caught the food, thinking would be a meal. it didn't.

fork.setup: a friend says: 'i read about meditation all week, so i'm basically calm now.' by the food story, what's the honest reply?
options: reading about it is like seeing food: real, but it doesn't fill you.
right: once the mind grasps an idea, the work is done.
reading is useless; only the body ever counts.
fork.reveal: in the Aitareya, the eye and the mind each reach for the food and stay hungry. one power alone, even a sharp mind, isn't the whole of it.

original.note: Sanskrit annam, food: what the self makes for the person, and what runs away in the Aitareya's story.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about food is a side note in a book about Brahman.
what it means: every power reaches for the food and fails alone; no one sense is the whole person.
what a scholar hears: Aitareya 1.3.1–10, where only apana, the in-drawing breath, seizes the food, just before the self asks how the body could run without it.
recall: dive to where the I rises

chat.meaning: In the Aitareya each power reaches for the food and none catches it alone. Each part is real; no single one is the whole person.

Aitareya Upanishad.meaning: the Upanishad that holds the great saying prajnanam brahma

apana.meaning: the breath that draws in and down; here, it takes food in

prajnanam brahma.meaning: the knowing is Brahman; one of the great sayings

Brahman.meaning: the Upanishads' word for the reality behind everything

mahavakyas.meaning: the great sayings, gathered by tradition from the Upanishads

sources.ref: Aitareya Upanishad 1.3.1–10 (the self creates food; the food turns and flees; the self tries to seize it with speech, breath, eye, ear, skin, mind and the rest, and fails, the text adding that otherwise one would be satisfied merely by speaking of, smelling, seeing, hearing, touching or thinking of food; it seizes it with apana)

notes: Block 'the four mahavakyas — prajnanam brahma', day 3 of 9 (1735–1743). 1735 set the four sayings side by side; 1736 told Aitareya 1.1–1.2 and 1.3.11–14 (the powers entering the person; 'then who am I?'; the crown). This day takes the passage between them, 1.3.1–10, so it doesn't repeat 1736.

Confirm the paraphrase of 1.3.3–10: the list in the text is speech, breath (prana: smelling), eye, ear, skin, mind, the generative organ, then apana; the voice names speech, breath, eye, ear, touch and mind and leaves out the generative organ. 'Apana, the breath that draws in and down' follows the common reading of apana here as the breath that takes food in; confirm the gloss.
